nameStory: The Shaggy Bracket gets its name from its distinctly fuzzy, hair-like surface that gives it a shaggy appearance - imagine a bracket fungus that needs a good haircut! This 'shaggy' texture comes from dense, bristle-like hairs that cover the upper surface of this shelf-like fungus.
description: The Shaggy Bracket is a shelf or bracket-shaped fungus that grows directly from the trunks and branches of hardwood trees, particularly oaks. It forms thick, robust brackets that can be quite substantial in size, with a characteristic fuzzy, hair-covered upper surface that feels rough to the touch. This fungus is actually a plant pathogen, meaning it attacks living trees and can cause significant damage to its hosts. The brackets have a woody, cork-like texture and appear as prominent shelves jutting out from tree bark.

idTips.label: Cap Surface
idTips.description: Densely covered with coarse, bristle-like hairs that give it a distinctly shaggy, fuzzy texture - run your hand over it and it feels like rough velvet or a stiff brush

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thick, bracket-like shelves that project horizontally from tree trunks, often overlapping in tiered formations

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underside has tiny pores instead of gills, initially cream-colored but bruising brown when touched or damaged

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels woody and cork-like when mature, becoming quite hard and persistent - like touching a piece of rough wood

idTips.label: Host Trees
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on living hardwood trees, especially oaks, where it causes heart rot and can seriously weaken the tree

habitat: Look for Shaggy Brackets on living hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, with a strong preference for oak species. They're commonly found in mature woodlands, parks, and anywhere old oaks grow, from coastal areas to inland forests. The fungus attacks living trees, so you'll typically spot them on trees that may show other signs of stress or disease.

seasonality.spring: New growth may begin appearing as small bumps on host trees. Existing brackets from previous years remain visible and can be examined for identification features.
seasonality.summer: Active growing season when fresh brackets develop their characteristic shaggy texture most prominently. The fuzzy surface is at its most distinctive during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Brackets reach full maturity and spore production peaks. This is often the best time to observe the complete range of identification features as brackets are fully developed.
seasonality.winter: Old brackets persist on trees and become harder and more woody, though still identifiable by their distinctive hairy surface texture even when weathered.

funFact: Despite being called a bracket fungus, the Shaggy Bracket is actually a tree assassin in disguise - it's one of the most destructive fungi to oak trees, causing a heart rot that can make seemingly healthy-looking trees extremely dangerous and prone to sudden failure during storms!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other bracket fungi, but the Shaggy Bracket's distinctively fuzzy, hair-covered surface makes it quite unique - if it feels shaggy and rough like a stiff brush, you've likely found your fungus. Other brackets tend to have smooth, velvety, or concentrically zoned surfaces rather than this bristly texture.
contextualKnowledge: This fungus is particularly important for arborists and tree care professionals to recognize, as its presence indicates significant structural compromise in the host tree. Property owners should be aware that trees with Shaggy Brackets may pose safety hazards and should be evaluated by tree care professionals.
compareHints: Unlike its relative Chaga which forms black, charcoal-like masses on birch trees, the Shaggy Bracket creates obvious shelf-like brackets with its signature fuzzy surface. Clustered Bracket forms smaller, overlapping brackets but lacks the distinctive shaggy hair covering, while other Inonotus species tend to have smoother surfaces and different host preferences.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relatives Shaggy Bracket and Clustered Bracket which form typical shelf-like fruiting bodies, chaga creates these unique charcoal-like sclerotia instead of normal mushroom structures.
